subject: redPanda
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: red panda balancing on a mossy stone.
Style: Genshin Impact.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module for a red panda on a mossy stone in a Genshin toon style, aiming for roughly 200 parts with helper functions while keeping the API usage correct and reasonably compact.

For the pose, I'm deciding on a quadruped standing stance with all four paws on a rounded boulder, tail curving up behind in an S-shape, head held up — balancing without lifting any limbs, keeping it a neutral rest pose. I'm working out proportions: a stylized red panda with body length around 0.55m, tail near 0.45m, shoulder height about 0.35m, standing on a boulder roughly 0.5m wide and 0.25m tall, with the stone bottom grounded at y=0 and the panda's feet resting on the stone's top surface.

Now I'm building the stone as a lathed, low-poly boulder with moss-mottled cel-shaded coloring on upward-facing surfaces and a greyish-blue stone tone elsewhere, adding a couple of smaller rock pieces for irregularity and a scalloped moss cap on top. I'm setting up the paint and color scheme to stay within the flat-color budget, then moving into defining the skeleton starting with a hips joint positioned relative to the stone's top height.

Working out the body proportions now: setting the spine height and radius for a fluffy panda torso spanning from hips to chest, then calculating leg lengths so the hind legs properly reach from the hip joint down to the stone's surface, using a three-segment limb setup for natural bending.

For hind legs with lengths [0.1,0.09,0.06], the vertical reach from hip to foot comes out quite short relative to total limb length, meaning the knee would need to fold very acutely. That seems too cramped, so I'm reconsidering raising the body height so hips sit higher and legs have more natural room to extend.

Front legs are only slightly bent, which looks fine for a standing rest pose. Now I'm sketching out the spine chain from hips through chest to neck and head, setting hips as the root joint with no parent, then building the rest of the skeletal hierarchy from there.

I'll keep hips as the root joint and let spine1 effectively coincide with it for simplicity. For the neck, I'll build a short chain from the chest position up to the head base using a 3-point catmull path split into "neck1" and "neck2", parented to spine3.

For the head, I'm placing a joint near the neck's end aimed slightly forward and down, then defining a head center offset forward to shape a wide red panda skull with cheek ruffs, a small snout, and round ears.

I'm planning out the facial details true to a real red panda — white cheek patches, rust crown, white-rimmed ears with dark interior, and dark tear marks running from eyes to muzzle. For the eyes I'm considering an anime-style sparkly eye decal with amber iris, sizing it proportionally against the head width.

Now I'm working out eye placement using spherical coordinates around the skull bone, mirroring decals for symmetry. I'm also sketching the muzzle as a cream-colored scaled sphere with a small dark nose tip, and setting up a separate jaw bone parented to the head for the mouth movement.

For the mouth, I'm deciding to skip a tongue but add a thin dark rod along the muzzle seam for the mouth line, and considering a few more thin rods for detail. Now I'm planning the ears as layered ellipsoids -- an outer cream rim and inner dark sphere, flattened and oriented, positioned symmetrically on the sides of the head.

Working out ear orientation and inner ear details...

For the stone scene decor, I'm thinking moss tufts and tiny glowing mushroom caps would add nice texture without overcomplicating things, and considering whether to give the panda a bamboo sprig nearby on the stone rather than near the face, since nothing should overlap the face itself.

For a Genshin-style accessory, I'm leaning toward a small teal scarf with gold trim looped around the neck, since the neck area is short and partly hidden by head fur anyway. Building the neck ring geometry...

For the body I want the sweep to follow the spine chain with rounded caps for a dome-like finish, using elliptical radii that taper slightly along the torso. For coloring, I'm thinking rust-orange on the back and dark brownish-black on the belly and legs to match the real red panda pattern, adapted into the Genshin palette.

I'm setting up a countershading transition with a zigzag edge between the rust back and dark belly tones, then considering adding some small fur tuft cards along the spine and cheeks using tinted SVG shapes for extra fluffiness.

For greys, I'll use white fill with lighter grey center lines. Now thinking through the tail: a long bushy red panda tail with rust and darker rings, curving upward behind the hips in a gentle S shape for a balancing pose, with four named tail segments chained from the hips.

Writing tail ring pattern...

Now for the legs: front legs angle from shoulders down to paws positioned forward, colored dark brownish-black with cel shading and cream-colored paw pads.

Adding toe spheres...

For hind legs I need four points: hip, knee, hock, and foot, giving three spans plus a tip, same as the front legs' three-point chain. I'll use the `limb` helper to generate the joint positions between root and target, then pass that point array into `chain` as a polyline.

Now I'm figuring out parenting: the front shoulder joint should attach to the spine joint whose z-range contains it (spine3, index 2), while the hind hip joint falls within spine1's range and should parent there instead.

For the body skin, I plan to sweep only the spine chain while keeping hips as a separate root bone, and extend the neck with a short three-point chain from the chest up to the head joint, with radii tapering so it's mostly covered by the ruff. The head joint sits at the end of the neck, parented to neck2, with its own orientation axis for placing head parts.

Now I'm sizing the head itself — making it a bit larger than the body radius for a cute proportion, roughly 0.115 wide, 0.092 tall, 0.1 deep, centered just above the neck end so it slightly overlaps the chest dome, which should look fine. I'm also positioning a small cream muzzle sphere offset from the head center to sit as the snout.

Now I'm placing the facial details: a small dark nose sphere near the muzzle tip, a lower jaw piece slightly below and forward, and considering whether the mouth should be open or closed (closed for now). For finer marks like a mouth seam, tear marks, and brow details, I'm thinking it'd be simpler to use a decal texture on the skull rather than modeling tiny geometric strokes.

I'm sketching the mouth as a simple ink-style curve on the muzzle decal, and designing a separate tear-mark decal — tapered dark-rust streaks running from the eye corners down toward the mouth, placed symmetrically at an angle below each eye, along with white eyebrow patches for the red panda's facial markings.

Now I'm working out the skull coloring: rust on the crown, cream on the lower face and cheeks, using a position-based fur edge split with a jagged boundary so the transition looks like natural fur rather than a hard line, then wrapping the whole thing in the cel/ink shading pass.

For the cheek ruffs, I'm planning cream tuft spikes positioned around the sides of the skull, angled outward and swept back, computing each spike's direction from the surface normal plus a backward bias so they read as fluffy fur tufts rather than straight cones.

Next I'm adding brow patches as small cream flattened sphere decals placed above the eyes, positioning them by azimuth and elevation on the head, then sizing the eye decals themselves and placing them symmetrically at roughly 34 degrees azimuth.

No glow needed. I'll go with an amber-brown iris "#a8561f" with lighter highlights "#ffd08a" rather than literal red panda dark brown, keeping the Genshin-style shine, and use a soft cream blush "#ff8f8f" positioned on the cheek. Now I'm working out the eye's vertical placement relative to the crown/cream boundary, calculating where the eye center and span land given the elevation angle.

I'm adjusting the boundary lower so the cream cheek ruff extends further down, and planning a white muzzle patch along with a dark tear-mark decal placed under the eye toward the muzzle. Now I'm setting up the ear geometry, positioning and orienting the ear spheres relative to the head center.

For the ear coloring, I'm layering an outer rust-red ellipsoid with a smaller cream ellipsoid offset forward to mimic the white inner fur, plus small cream tufts on top, and defining the orientation so the ear's local z-axis points along the computed direction. Next I'm thinking through the rust-colored crown marking on the forehead.

I'm adding a few small rust cone tufts for the crown, thin cream whisker rods from the muzzle, and a teal scarf with gold trim wrapped around the neck, working out the neck's position and direction vector to orient the collar ring correctly.

Since the scarf would end up hidden inside the head geometry if placed directly at the neck, I'm repositioning it to the chest-neck junction instead, checking that this spot still avoids colliding with the head's lower ellipsoid edge.

Now I'm working out the hanging scarf ends: a knot sphere on the chest front with two extruded ribbon tails and gold tassels, figuring out the plane and thickness for the extrusion and where the knot point sits relative to the chest surface.

Since the chest curves backward at the base, I'm angling the ribbons slightly inward and backward so they drape naturally rather than floating in front of the belly, splitting the two tails outward with a slight tilt as they hang down.

The non-orthogonal basis vectors should still work fine even if slightly sheared. I'll keep the scarf accessory plus add a small gold bell charm for extra detail, then move to shaping the stone — using a lathe for the main asymmetric body with an offset lump, colored through cel-shading and noise paint, with a profile defining the rounded silhouette.

I need the stone radius to be large enough to cover the panda's footprint, including front and hind paws plus the tail overhang, so I'm considering whether the lathe output supports scaling to elongate the stone shape appropriately.

I'm worried about whether mesh scaling survives the export's matrix baking process, but decide the safer route is constructing the geometry directly with three.js's LatheGeometry, applying a manual scale to the geometry itself, then passing it to the part function with paint intact since it reads from positions rather than UVs.

For the lathe profile, I need points ordered bottom-to-top so the normals face outward correctly, starting near the axis and ending at the top. I'm also thinking about jittering vertices afterward for a rocky texture, but noting that lathe geometry duplicates seam vertices at the start/end angle, which complicates per-vertex randomization.

Using a position-based sine displacement instead of random noise keeps the duplicated seam vertices consistent since the function only depends on x/y/z, not vertex index. I want flat shading to give the faceted stone look, with displacement mostly radial and limited near the top so the cap stays relatively flat, then plan a second lathe for a mossy drooping cap and decide moss placement based on normal y-value.

I'm defining color palettes for moss and stone, then writing the paint function that blends normal direction, noise, and height to decide whether each surface point gets mossy green or stony gray tones...

Now I'm wrapping the stone paint with the cel shading function for toon-style lighting, and thinking about scattering small moss tuft cards across the top of the stone where it's flat enough, being careful to keep them away from where the panda's feet would intersect.

For the moss tufts I'm setting up card sizes and flow direction, with tilt and variation so they don't look uniform, using two tint colors for variety and a grey gradient for the card fill. I'm also adding a few small glowing mushrooms near the stone's front-right using lathe geometry for cream stems and glowing orange caps.

Now I'm working through the body coloring, using cel-shaded edges with a rust-to-dark-belly gradient and dark brown fur for the legs, blending into rust tones near the top where the leg meets the body.

I'm also checking on texture budget — making sure the paint resolution is dense enough to handle both the character details and the large stone surface without stretching thin.

For the texture list, I'm sorting out which elements need painted texture versus simple decals: eyes, tears, mouth get decals, fur gets card textures, and scarf ribbons get painted patterns since extrude geometry only supports paints, not standalone textures.

So that's six textures total: eye, tear, mouth, tuft, grass, and emblem. For the tail, I'm scattering fur tuft cards along the tail surface with a rust tint, thinking through how the flow direction should follow the tail's tangent toward the tip rather than using the default downward flow, though I could just keep it simple with a default lean angle instead.

Now I'm defining the body fur scatter filtered to upward-facing normals, plus a separate cheek ruff scatter on the skull sides for cream-colored tufts, making sure the filter avoids overlapping the eyes.

Adding haunch and shoulder bulge spheres attached to the hip and shoulder joints for fluffy thigh volume, then setting up jaw and head joint roles for the rest pose skeleton.

I'm now defining joint roles for the spine, neck, tail, and legs, then building the body using a sweep function along the spine with smooth circular cross-sections for a cel-shaded coat look, keeping continuity through the chest and neck.

I'm calculating radius functions for the body's width and height to give it a slight chubby curve, positioning the spine within the correct height range, and working out foot target positions and leg chain lengths so the limbs connect naturally to the hips and shoulders.

Now I'm figuring out paw placement geometry, aligning the paw sphere's center and scale so it rests properly on the ground relative to the ankle target, then setting up the hind leg root and target positions for a plantigrade stance with forward-extending feet.

Checking the hock positioning — knee forward, hock back, with cannon roughly vertical seems reasonable given the chain geometry. I'm sanity-checking leg sweep radii and hip offset against the body's half-width to make sure proportions stay sensible.

Widening leg stance now: hips at ±0.1, shoulders ±0.095, feet ±0.11. For toes, I'm placing three small flattened spheres per paw offset slightly in x, colored dark, skipping claws and toe beans for simplicity. For the tail, I'm working out the joint path starting near the rear of the body dome and building outward from there.

Tail curves upward into an S-shape for balance, with radii tapering from thick near the base to thin at the tip—fluffy and proportional to the body width. I'm adding nine painted rings along the tail length, with the final stretch past 92% marked as a dark tip band, making sure the tip height stays within the character's overall bounds.

Checking the overall proportions: tail tip reaches about 0.8, head and ears top out near 0.72, panda stands roughly 0.5m above the stone base. The stone footprint is lathed with a stretched elliptical radius, and I'm centering it around the panda's feet to make sure nothing overhangs awkwardly.

I want the stone's top surface to stay flat where the panda's paws rest, so I'm keeping the perturbation displacement purely radial and zeroing out vertical displacement near the top ring. I'm adding a subtle dome to the top profile with slight y variation across the radius so it doesn't look perfectly flat while still supporting the paws correctly.

I'll also toss in a small secondary pebble or rock lump near the base of the main stone to break up the composition without overcomplicating the geometry.

Now I'm verifying that everything sits flush at floor level—the stone profile starts at y=0 and the lumps sink just slightly to avoid any visible gap. Next I'll move on to building the mushroom stems.

Placing the mushroom cluster on the front-left face where the panda faces, with three different-sized mushrooms at varied azimuths and elevations, glowing orange caps and cream stems offset slightly outward along the surface normal from their stem positions.

I'm also adding small Sweet Flower-style elements near the stone's edges—flat textured cards with white petals scattered around the top ring, filtered to appear only near the outer boundary away from the center cluster.

With part budget looking reasonable (around 130-200 pieces), I'm now moving into writing the actual code, starting with imports for the geometry builder, toon shading kit, and glow effects.

Now I'm defining the color palette with rust oranges, cream tones for the belly, deep shadows, and accent colors like teal and gold for highlights.

I'm setting up the fur edge coat paint with a countershading transition between the rust upper coat and darker belly, tuning the blend level, tooth pattern, and ink outline color so the shading reads naturally across the body's surface normal.

Now I'm defining the leg and head coat paints using gradients and fur-edge blends between rust, dark, and cream tones, wrapping each in the shading function so the colors resolve with proper shadow treatment.

For the ears, I'm planning a rust outer surface with cream inner coloring, and setting up a simple paint helper function to keep the code concise as I continue defining the surface materials.

Starting the build function for the red panda scene, setting up a seeded random generator for jittering details and beginning to establish the basic constants and structure.

Building the joint skeleton...

Defining more joints...

For the tail color, I'm setting up a banding pattern using a zigzag function along the tail's length to alternate between two ring colors, with a special tip color at the very end.

Now I'm moving to building the leg chains, looping over left and right sides to define shoulder and foot points for front legs, then creating bone chains parented to the spine joints.

I'm also working through how the bend parameter should be formatted — whether it's a single direction vector or a list of direction vectors depending on how many inner joints the limb has, and deciding to pass it as a single array for the two-segment legs.

For the chain sweep I'm confirming that the leg geometry accepts a path input and radius array, then planning a small helper function to create fluffy shoulder blobs using sphere geometry attached to a bone with configurable color and position.

For the paw I'm attaching a dark blob to the wrist joint at the end of the leg chain, pulling that joint reference from the last element of the chain's joints array, then setting up three flattened toe spheres positioned on that same wrist bone.

Now I'm building the hind leg chain with hip, knee, hock, and foot joints parented to the spine, making sure the names array matches the span count plus tip. For the hind paw I'm extending the blob further back to form a plantigrade heel shape.

Adding the haunch and shoulder blobs positioned at the hip and shoulder joints with rust coloring, then moving on to define the skull as a scaled sphere attached to the head bone.

For the surface mesh, I'm setting up a `skin` surface wrapper around the skull so I can place features using angular coordinates — I need to be careful that the center point used for `.around()` stays inside the skull geometry so it doesn't return null. I'm starting to position the eyes using the animated eye helper, placing them symmetrically using azimuth and elevation offsets around the head center.

Adding decals for the eyes...

Now I'm double-checking whether decals should target the raw surface or the skull part itself, deciding to pass the skull part directly like the reference example does, and starting to think about adding a tear texture decal next.

Adjusting brow spot placement and size to avoid overlapping the eye decals, raising the elevation and shifting azimuth inward so they sit cleanly above the eyes.

Now I'm working out the muzzle geometry—placing a cream-colored blob offset forward and down from the head center, adding a flattened nose shape at the front tip, and checking the muzzle width stays proportional to the head. I'm also starting on a mouth decal texture with ink-stroke SVG paths for the philtrum and lip lines.

Placing the mouth decal on the muzzle surface...

Adding whisker rods on each side of the muzzle, then thinking through ear details—small cream fur tufts as spikes positioned around the front-lower rim of each ear.

Now I'm placing cheek ruffs: a set of spikes at various angles and elevations around the face, pointing outward and back to create a furry ruff effect.

That checks out around 0.113. Now I'm scattering fur card tufts across the cheeks and skull surface, filtering by normal direction and position to avoid overlaps, with cream and rust tints for variation. I'm also planning a few crown-area spikes before moving on to the scarf geometry.

Building the scarf ring...

Checking the top point of the scarf ring against the head position, I find it doesn't actually intersect since the head's minimum z is further forward. The scarf sits just above the shoulders like a proper collar, though I'm considering nudging the ring center down slightly to align better with the neck.

Now I'm adding a gold trim: two thinner rings offset forward and backward from the main scarf ring to mark front and back edges, plus a knot sphere positioned at the front-lower point of the scarf to anchor the ribbon detail.

Actually this confirms the issue: the neck direction I'm using is nearly horizontal, not vertical, which means the ring plane orientation needs rethinking since the scarf should wrap around a mostly-forward-pointing neck rather than an upright one.

The ribbons should hang freely between the front legs beneath the chest, which looks cute and natural given the leg positions. I'm computing the knot position programmatically by offsetting from the neck point along a flattened up-vector perpendicular to the body's normal.

Now I'm working out the emblem and ribbon geometry: a small gold-colored disc plane for the emblem sits just in front of the teal knot sphere, while the ribbon shapes extrude from outline curves positioned symmetrically on either side of the knot.

I'm checking the ribbon's orientation vectors to make sure its thickness axis points correctly, then tracing how the bottom endpoints move — realizing the current direction sends them forward instead of backward like I want.

I flip the y-direction so it curves down and back to hug the belly, and sketch out a paint function that colors most of the ribbon teal but turns gold near the edges and tail end.

Rather than a tassel, I decide to add a small gold bell charm near the knot, attached to the spine bone along with the rest of the ribbon pieces. For the stone, I'll rig it to the hips bone so it stays fixed relative to the panda's root.

Now I'm writing the lathe-based rock geometry function that jitters vertex positions with layered sine/cosine noise to break up the perfect radial symmetry...

I'm weighing whether the degenerate triangle at the lathe profile's starting point could cause UV or baking issues, and considering nudging the profile start away from zero to avoid a zero-area UV triangle -- though I realize that might just open an unwanted hole at the top or bottom instead, since both ends need to stay effectively closed or hidden.

I decide the degenerate triangle from a zero-radius hole is probably harmless for texture baking, but to be safe I'll just use a small nonzero radius like 0.004 to avoid the issue entirely. I'm now sketching the stone's radius profile as a series of points moving from the center outward and up to form its curved shape.

Checking the panda's paw positions against the lathe-space radius confirms they stay within the stone's silhouette, and I'm noting that the moss cap will be handled with card geometry rather than extra overhang lumps -- using icosahedron shapes scaled down for small rock lumps.

I'm positioning three small lump decorations around the base at varying coordinates and scales, verifying their bottom edges sink only slightly below the stone surface to stay within tolerance, then checking the icosahedron's vertex extents to confirm placement accuracy.

Now I'm moving on to the moss texture SVG, designing curved grass blade shapes with layered white and grey fills for a natural look.

Still writing SVG icons...

I'm scattering fur tufts across the body surface, using a seeded distribution filtered to avoid the underside, then rendering them as small leaning cards with bend and color variation to create a backward-swept fur texture. One thing I'm noting is that the flat tuft colors might clash with the cel-shaded body rendering.

For the tail, I'm scattering lighter-tinted cards, reducing their count and size so they don't fully obscure the ring pattern underneath. I'm now sketching out a rough part count tally covering the body, neck, tail, and legs to keep track of total geometry.

Tallying up the rest: paws with toes, layered ears, facial features like eyes, brows, muzzle, cheek spikes, whiskers, scarf rings, stone chunks, and mushroom caps brings the total to around 80 parts. Since the target range is flexible, I want to push detail further by adding claws, ear tufts, forehead spikes, tail tip tufts, and belly fur to make the creature feel richer.

Now I'm figuring out how to scatter small decorative elements like pebbles, ferns, and moss clumps along the stone's rim, using raycasts from above to find the surface and stick flattened moss spheres onto it at varied angles and radii around the edge.

Setting up the moss color palette with cel-shaded flat tones, then defining a sticker helper that embeds small parts along surface normals with squish scaling. I'm sketching out the color constants at the top using the cel-shading helper for rust tones and double-checking the part/paint/texture signature before moving on.

Now I'm defining a hit-point tuple type for coordinates and a helper function that offsets from a base coordinate, plus starting a sphere geometry and blob helper for constructing rounded shapes...

Adding ear geometry with layered blobs...

I'm reasoning through how the offset helper and directional orientation interact for positioning the ear shapes, and double-checking the ear's placement against the skull's top-lateral coordinates.

I'm working out that the ear center sits slightly outside the ideal skull boundary, which is fine for embedding, and that the ear's local orientation uses the projected up-axis correctly. I'm also planning the fur detail — white tufts inside the ears, rust-colored outer coloring, and a few small rust-colored crown spikes pointing up and back from the top of the head.

I decide the chest and tail root don't need extra special-casing since red pandas have dark chests, and the default pose for the front legs angled slightly outward works fine. I settle on teal and gold cel-shaded color pairs for the scarf accents, then start writing a helper function for generating fur tufts/spikes along a bone. Writing tuft helper function...

I need to handle nullable results from the panda's surface lookups, skipping gracefully if a hit is missing. For whiskers, jaw, and neck details I'm deciding which small features to actually build versus skip for simplicity—fangs, tongue, and neck fluff aren't worth the complexity, while fur cards and rod-based whiskers get added using the skin and scatter helpers. I'm also setting up a ray query against the rock surface to position things correctly on terrain.

Now I'm working out mushroom placement, computing ray hits around the stone's surface at various azimuth and elevation angles to make sure they land on the slope near the front where the panda is positioned.

Checking that the cap embed and color setup work correctly with glow and flat material types, then planning flower placement using scattered hits along the stone top rim.

Still writing scatter filters...

I'm counting up the distinct textures and tints needed—grass tints, tuft colors for body/tail/cheeks/crown, plus flower, eye, tear, mouth, and emblem—roughly 13 entries total, which should pack fine into a 4096 atlas. I'm trimming the eye texture size down to 320 to save space, and considering whether to skip adding a held bamboo leaf or floating accent element.

Now I'm defining the color palette with cel-shaded lit/shadow pairs for rust, cream, dark, teal, and gold tones, then setting up the coat shading function with fur edge effects and ink outline colors.

Working out leg and tail gradients, mapping gradient positions to top and bottom colors, then starting the moss/stone color definitions...

Adding stone surface paint logic...

Still setting up imports and color constants...

Continuing the sweep profiles for neck and tail with smooth radius transitions, then working out hip joint positions and offsets for the hind legs, checking the head bone eye decal placement, and setting up the scarf's anchor point coordinates.

Now I'm defining the scarf's loop geometry around the neck using a ring frame and sweeping both the main teal band and the thinner gold trim loops along it, bound to the neck bone.

Good, the gold trim sits right against the teal edge so the radii line up. Now I'm computing the knot position by projecting an up vector perpendicular to the neck direction, then placing a small sphere there for the scarf knot, working through the coordinate math to get its exact position.

Next I'm positioning an emblem disc just in front of the knot sphere, checking that its z-depth clears the sphere's surface so it reads as sitting on top rather than inside it. Then I'm starting to lay out the ribbon extrusions hanging from the knot...

Writing ribbon outline shape...

Writing moss clump placement loop...

I'll trim the radius slightly to avoid overlapping paws, and need to guard against a null hit from the ray cast. I'm also adding flat shading for the stone and lumps for a low-poly look, and double-checking that closed sweeps and ring joints weld properly, plus making sure SVG strings include the right namespace.

For the decals, I'm sketching a teardrop shape SVG scaled to size 128, and a mouth decal at viewBox 64x40 scaled up to 192, adjusting stroke widths to match each scale factor.

Now I'm working out positioning parameters for the mouth decal on the muzzle, calculating the exact height offset so it sits just outside the surface, then placing mirrored tear decals near the eyes using skin coordinates with alternating mirror flags based on side.

Next I'm defining the jaw joint parented to the head, setting its pivot and aim point, then considering a small pink tongue blob but deciding to skip it since the muzzle already covers that area—keeping the part count efficient.

Then I'm thinking through the tail tip tuft: trying to place five small spikes radiating from the tail's end point, considering using a ring primitive along the tail chain but deciding that's risky, so instead planning to manually position each spike using the tail's tangent direction at its endpoint.

Next I'm planning the claws: three small cream cone shapes per paw, angled forward-down from the wrist bone with a tapered, low-poly look.

Finally I'm setting up the tail chain structure itself, parenting it to the hips joint and defining the path and joint names so it segments properly from the tail base near the hips.
